newsitem.title: SWITZERLAND: Holocaust factor weighs on Swiss financial markets.
newsitem.headline: Holocaust factor weighs on Swiss financial markets.

text.p: Allegations that Swiss banks plundered unclaimed wealth of Holocaust victims have thrown a small but persistent degree of uncertainty into Swiss financial markets, economists and analysts said on Wednesday.
Markets have not sustained any lasting damage so far from a painful subject which will likely take years to resolve, but they have been hit on a day-to-day basis by rumours and news.

Stocks of the big three banks, Credit Suisse -- Union Bank of Switzerland (UBS) and Swiss Bank Corp (SBC) -- fell on Monday after Jewish organisations renewed threats to boycott Swiss financial institutions.

Banks shares recovered by Wednesday, helped by a Swiss government statement that it wanted to begin immediate talks with banks and Jewish groups on using dormant Swiss accounts to create a memorial fund for Nazi victims.
A decision is expected by the end of January.
Madeleine Hofmann, banking analyst at Credit Suisse, said that the boycott threats, if put into practice, could theoretically cause significant damage.
Such a boycott could also involve withdrawing funds managed by the banks under private banking activities.
"The big Swiss banks derive roughly 50 percent of their profits from their private banking activities," Hofmann said.
"If this area were affected, then that would certainly be negative, because that is an important business," she said.
But even if a boycott were to be agreed in theory, it may be difficult to enforce in practice, she added.
Swiss share markets also did not appear to be valuing the banks as if they expected major losses from any boycott.
The issue of the Holocaust funds is an emotional one, making it difficult to evaluate its impact objectively.

Analysts normally used to mulling fundamentals are now weighing moral issues and what critics say is Switzerland's belated effort to satisfy Jews and other Nazi victims who lost their wealth in the war.

Emotions flared after outgoing Economics Minister Jean-Pascal Delamuraz, on his last day in office as Swiss president, described as "blackmail" Jewish groups' call for a fund to compensate Nazi victims.
The Swiss franc, which is often volatile compared with more liquid currencies, has also suffered ups and downs linked to the issue, which are expected to remain a factor for months.

It fell in December on the mistaken belief that Switzerland would abolish banking secrecy laws to let an independent panel search for unclaimed Holocaust-era bank accounts. Such a move would have stripped Switzerland of a big competitive advantage.
Switzerland in fact had loosened secrecy laws only for accounts set up just before and during World War Two.

One London-based currency analyst said talk about secrecy laws may have been a trigger for the franc's declines, but its reasons for weakening appeared to more fundamental. These include the Swiss National Bank's pro-growth monetary policy.

"The questions in terms of the Holocaust are significant and serious things that need to be addresed," the analyst said. "But their macroeconomic effect on the franc is probably limited. I think probably their impact on sentiment is mainly short-term."
Some Swiss analysts say sensitivity to the issues by the government and banks will be a key factor.

"If they can show the other side this matter is being dealt with seriously, with the whole problem set in its moral dimension, then we should have this problem cleared quickly from the market," Swiss Bank Corp economist Jan Acket said.
-- Zurich Editorial, +41 1 631 7340
